inputs.label: Parcelbird briefing pack (evidence/briefing-pack.md)
inputs.content:
# Parcelbird: should we launch 15-minute grocery delivery? — briefing pack

> **Synthetic benchmark data.** The company, people, competitors and every figure in this pack are fictional. They were generated for a reasoning benchmark and are internally consistent, but they are not real market data.

## 1. Context

Parcelbird, founded in 2023 in Columbus, Ohio, sells software that runs small grocery fulfillment sites (inventory,
picking, rider dispatch) to grocers. ARR is $4.1M, growing 60% a year, gross margin 81%. The company has $12.0M in
cash and burns $0.4M a month.

The founders now propose that Parcelbird become an operator itself: launch **Parcelbird Now**, a 15-minute grocery
delivery service from its own dark stores in Columbus, Indianapolis and Kansas City.

**Decision maker:** the board (two founders and two investors), January 2027.

## 2. Decision question

**Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce grocery delivery service in 2027?**

## 3. Objectives and constraints

- The investors want a path to profitability within the current cash; a new funding round for a delivery
  operator is "unlikely in this market", according to the lead investor.
- Keep at least 12 months of runway at all times.

## 4. The founders' view

"Quick commerce is growing over 40% a year and nobody owns the Midwest. Our software already runs other people's
dark stores, so we know how to run them better than anyone. With density, the unit economics turn positive: our
model shows contribution profit per order by month 18."

## 5. Market

**Table 1. US quick-commerce grocery sales (GMV), $ billions**

| 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.8 | 2.6 | 3.6 | 5.1 |

**Table 2. Incumbent operators (2025)**

| Operator | Revenue | EBITDA | Contribution per order |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zipcart (national) | $1,200M | −$310M | −$1.90 |
| QuickBasket (regional) | $210M | −$96M | −$3.40 |

QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities in 2025.

## 6. Unit economics

**Table 3. Per-order inputs: industry benchmarks from Parcelbird's software customers (14 sites, 2025) and the founders' plan**

| Input | Benchmark median | Best observed site | Founders' plan |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average order value (AOV) | $34 | $42 | $45 |
| Gross margin on goods | 27% | 27% | 27% |
| Delivery fee collected per order, net of payment cost on it | $1.99 | $1.99 | $1.99 |
| Picking and packing labor per order | $3.10 | $3.10 | $3.10 |
| Rider cost per hour (wage, insurance, vehicle) | $17.75 | $17.75 | $17.75 |
| Orders delivered per rider-hour | 2.4 | 3.0 | 3.5 |
| Dark-store fixed cost per site per year (rent, staff, utilities) | $1.15M | $1.15M | $1.15M |
| Orders per site per day | 900 | 1,400 | 1,800 |
| Payment processing and packaging per order | $1.30 | $1.30 | $1.30 |
| Promotions and discounts, % of AOV | 6% | 6% | 2% |

The best observed AOV and the best observed density are from different sites; no site achieved both. The
benchmark range for orders per rider-hour is 1.9–3.0 and for orders per site per day 400–1,400.

## 7. Columbus pop-up test (six weeks, one temporary site, autumn 2026)

- 11,800 orders; AOV $31; orders grew 18% a week on average.
- Promotions averaged 12% of AOV; riders delivered 2.1 orders per hour; the site averaged 280 orders a day;
  the temporary site's annualised fixed cost was $650,000.

## 8. Customers

- Survey of 1,500 Columbus residents aged 25–39: 44% said they would use 15-minute delivery "at least weekly".
- Pop-up customer data: customer acquisition cost $38 (paid social and first-order credits); 22% of customers
  still ordering in month three; those customers ordered 3.1 times a month.

## 9. Capital

- Founders' plan: 9 dark stores at $0.6M capex each ($5.4M), and a total of $9.5M of cash needed to month 18
  (capex, launch marketing, operating losses), against $12.0M in the bank.

## 10. The software business

- 37 grocers are in the sales pipeline for the software, 9 at the late stage; average contract value $96,000 a year.
- Several grocers in the pipeline want to launch their own fast delivery from existing stores.
- Scaling the software business would need 2 more engineers and 2 sales hires (about $0.8M a year).

## 11. Other material

- **Founders' investor update:** "Zipcart turned contribution-positive in its densest city in Q4 2025 (+$0.40 per
  order). It can be done." Zipcart's shareholder letter adds that this followed a new $3.99 service fee on every
  order and a cut in promotions to 1% of order value, and that order volume in that city fell 14% afterwards.

## 12. Uncertainties

- Whether density in mid-size Midwest cities can reach the benchmark median.
- Whether AOV can rise without losing the convenience use case.
- Rider labor rules: two of the three cities are considering minimum pay standards for delivery workers.

storyline.governing_thought: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027: it loses money on every order and breaks the runway rule; sell fast-delivery software to grocers instead

exec_summary.text: Quick commerce is growing fast, but its operators lose money on every order

sub_points.text: US sales reached $5.1B in 2025, 2.8 times the 2022 level
Zipcart loses $1.90 and QuickBasket $3.40 on each order

exec_summary.text: A dark store loses money at every level reached so far, and pop-up customers did not stay

sub_points.text: The median customer site loses $6.17 per order, the best site $1.76
Only the founders' plan, above the best site on four inputs, is positive
Only 22% of pop-up customers still ordered in month three

exec_summary.text: The launch breaks the 12-month runway rule, with no new funding in sight

sub_points.text: The plan plus today's burn leaves cash $4.7M short by month 18
Even the kindest reading leaves about 6 months of runway at month 18

exec_summary.text: Selling fast-delivery software to grocers captures the same demand for $1.2M

sub_points.text: Late-stage grocers would add $864K a year, 21% of today's ARR
A one-store pilot would cost $3.6M to retest what we already know

next_steps.action: Decline the 2027 launch of Parcelbird Now and approve 2 engineers and 2 sales hires ($0.8M a year)
Close the 9 late-stage grocers and scope fast delivery from grocers' own stores with them
Set a burn plan that keeps 12 months of runway beyond month 18
Revisit operating only if a customer site turns positive per order after site cost for two quarters

sources.name: Team analysis of the Parcelbird briefing pack

constraints.item: Keep at least 12 months of runway at all times
constraints.effect: today's burn alone reaches the floor at month 18, so the launch breaks it; the title of the cash page and exec item 3 say so

constraints.item: No new funding round for a delivery operator
constraints.effect: the plan must fit today's $12.0M; stated on p. 8

constraints.item: Today's $0.4M monthly burn, not in the founders' $9.5M
constraints.effect: adds $7.2M over 18 months; the kinder reading (already included) still leaves about 6 months of runway

constraints.item: Minimum pay standards for riders under discussion in two of three cities
constraints.effect: would raise rider cost, already the largest line; not sized because the pack gives no rate

constraints.item: Volume loss after a service fee (Zipcart: −14%)
constraints.effect: included in the Zipcart-fix estimate, which stays negative

constraints.item: Cost of the software hires ($0.8M a year)
constraints.effect: the software option is shown with its $1.2M 18-month cost and the note that it holds only if late-stage deals close

alternatives.option: Pilot one permanent dark store in Columbus before deciding on nine
alternatives.why: about $3.6M over 18 months at median economics to retest what 14 customer sites and the pop-up already show, and it breaks the runway floor unless burn falls

alternatives.option: Launch with Zipcart's fix: a $3.99 service fee and promotions cut to 1%
alternatives.why: the median site still loses about $1 per order after the 14% volume loss

alternatives.option: Software-first: fund the hires and sell fast delivery from grocers' own stores
alternatives.why: lowest cash need, 81% gross margin, revenue already in the late-stage pipeline

failure_threshold.driver: contribution per order after site cost (rider productivity the most sensitive input)
failure_threshold.threshold: the launch case turns right only if riders reach about 4.3 orders an hour at the best site's order value and density, against a best observed 3.0
failure_threshold.range: low −$12.57 (pop-up) / base −$6.17 (benchmark median) / high +$2.02 (founders' plan, every input above the best site)

consistency.headline: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027: it loses money on every order and breaks the runway rule; sell fast-delivery software to grocers instead
consistency.fix: Software-first is described as near the floor, holding only if late-stage deals close early and burn edges down, since today's burn alone reaches the floor at month 18
